A private meeting during the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale helped reshape the men's professional golf landscape , with the Asian Tour turning away from LIV Golf and striking a new agreement with the DP World Tour and PGA Tour.

The dramatic change followed the Public Investment Fund's decision to withdraw its multi-billion-dollar backing from LIV Golf. For the Asian Tour, which had developed a close relationship with LIV through the International Series, the news arrived at an especially difficult moment.

Asian Tour chief executive Cho Minn Thant said discussions about extending the partnership were still underway around the Masters.

"It was the week right after the Masters when LIV Golf was in Mexico. We found out at that time," Cho said.

The uncertainty went beyond LIV itself. Asian Tour officials initially did not know whether the withdrawal would also affect the International Series, or how quickly the funding would disappear.

"It was a really abrupt thing that happened, and it was very surprising news because, up until the Masters, we were still talking to LIV Golf about the next few years of a partnership," Cho explained. "We were talking about expanding the International Series, and it came as a total surprise."

Asian Tour Scrambles After LIV Golf Funding Shock

The Asian Tour began 2026 expecting a 21-event schedule and was looking toward another five years alongside LIV. Instead, the lucrative 10-event International Series was disbanded, leaving officials scrambling to protect the remainder of the calendar.

Planned tournaments in China and India will not take place. The Philippine Open will remain on the Asian Tour schedule in November, though with reduced prize money, while the Saudi International continues as a $5 million event.

Faced with that upheaval, Cho began exploring alternatives almost immediately.

"We've been talking since April," he said of negotiations with the DP World Tour and PGA Tour. "When the news broke, I had to pivot and start talking to the DP World Tour and PGA Tour."

Meetings followed in May and June before the decisive discussions took place at Royal Birkdale during the Open Championship.

"Then at the Open Championship we were able to agree to broad terms," Cho said.

Importantly, the Asian Tour had not immediately ruled out continuing with LIV. Cho said officials remained in contact with the league while monitoring its attempts to obtain new financing.

But the Asian Tour had schedules to build and players who needed tournaments.

"We just couldn't wait any longer," Cho said. "We had the second half of the schedule on the Asian Tour to get on with. We already planned events in 2027."

Royal Birkdale Deal Leaves LIV Without Its Feeder Circuit

Under the new arrangement, the Asian Tour will co-sanction five tournaments with the DP World Tour, including the Hong Kong Open and Singapore Open. Those tournaments are expected to feature split fields, with approximately 50 to 60 Asian Tour positions available.

The deal also strengthens the route from Asia to the DP World Tour. In addition to the Asian Tour Order of Merit winner earning a DP World Tour card, players will have five co-sanctioned opportunities to win and move directly onto the European circuit.

That helps protect opportunities for the Asian Tour's leading players. However, Cho acknowledged there is still work to do for golfers further down the membership list who benefited from the larger purses and opportunities the International Series provided.

For LIV Golf, meanwhile, losing the Asian Tour partnership creates another complication at a particularly difficult time.

The Asian Tour had effectively provided LIV with an important second-tier structure, including promotion and relegation opportunities. Its national opens were also expected to play a role as LIV attempted to build a schedule after losing PIF backing.

LIV's proposed "2.0" model now has to operate without that established feeder circuit, potentially complicating its efforts to maintain a structure compatible with world ranking points.

Cho said LIV chief executive Scott O'Neil wanted the Asian Tour to remain involved and presented proposals concerning future investment. Walking away was therefore not an easy decision.

"The International Series meant so much to us," Cho said. "It was a tough decision. LIV Golf were good partners."

LIV players are expected to receive opportunities at Asian Tour events, including the Hong Kong Open, while invitations will also be available for the Saudi International and Philippine Open. Many LIV golfers remain Asian Tour members.

"I expect quite a few of them to play on the Asian Tour next year," Cho said.

Cho Maps Out the Asian Tour's Post-LIV Rebuild

Despite the abrupt ending, Cho's assessment of the five-year relationship was straightforward. He credited the LIV-backed investment with improving fields, increasing prize money and raising the Asian Tour's standing within professional golf.

Now comes the harder part: replacing what disappeared.

Players have understandably been concerned. Cho addressed the entire membership at an AGM, explaining the loss of PIF and LIV sponsorship, the new agreements with the DP World Tour and PGA Tour, and plans for rebuilding the schedule.

The immediate objective is stability, not an overnight replacement for everything the International Series provided.

"We're going to take the rest of 2026 and 2027 as rebuilding years and hopefully back to full strength in 2028," Cho said.

The Asian Tour's relationship with the established tours has also changed sharply. During its LIV partnership, the circuit could be viewed as a competitor to the DP World Tour. Following the collapse of its previous funding arrangement, those old battle lines have shifted.

Cho described the decision in practical terms.

"I just think we have to adapt to whatever the market dictates," he said. "I don't think there's any feeling of resentment or anything like that."

He still regards the Asian Tour as Asia's premier circuit, while acknowledging that it currently sits below the PGA Tour and DP World Tour in the professional hierarchy.

His longer-term target is ambitious but specific: rebuild the Asian Tour to between 25 and 28 tournaments and establish it as what he described as "legitimately the third biggest tour in the world."

Only months earlier, the Asian Tour was discussing an expanded International Series and another five years alongside LIV Golf. By the time the Open Championship arrived at Royal Birkdale, its leadership was negotiating a very different future.

The agreement reached there gave the Asian Tour a route forward. For LIV, it removed a partner that had been deeply embedded in its plans, and left its post-PIF rebuilding effort with another major problem to solve.

articles.title: Former MI6 spy takes Trump to Scottish court for £800,000 legal payout
articles.summary: Christopher Steele was the author of a salacious "dossier" linking Trump to Russia during his 2016 election campaign.
articles.body:
A company founded by a former spy is pursuing Donald Trump at a small Scottish court for more than £800,000 in unpaid legal costs.

The US president was named in a hearing at Ayr Sheriff Court as Orbis Business Intelligence seeks funds from the Trump Turnberry golf resort.

The case concerns legal costs owed by Trump from a 2024 English data protection case against Orbis's director Christopher Steele - a former MI6 agent.

But SLC Turnberry Limited - which owns the course - is disputing Trump's role as the "ultimate owner", arguing that his stake in the course is held by a trust.

Steele was the author of a salacious "dossier" linking Trump to Russia during his 2016 election campaign.

London's High Court of Justice ruled Trump's action out of time and a judge ordered him to pay Orbis £680,000 in legal costs.

Orbis is targeting the president's financial interests at Turnberry in order to claim the funds.

The case called at Ayr Sheriff Court because the resort falls within its jurisdiction, while Steele and Orbis have no connections there.

More stories from Glasgow & West Scotland

Sheriff officers served papers at the Trump Turnberry resort last September.

Court documents named Trump as a "debtor" and reveal that, due to interest, the amount sought by two applications brought by Orbis totals £789,812.

In an online procedural hearing Orbis's advocate Duncan Hamilton KC stated that, despite an English court ordering the president to pay money to Orbis, "over the last 18 months since the last judgement, he has refused or failed to do so".

Due to interest accruing, he said, the costs now claimed by his client were now "north of £800,000" and that the applicant had spent "a great deal of time and money chasing president Trump in various jurisdictions."

Hamilton continued: "President Trump has stated emphatically that he owns Turnberry.

"He has committed that to federal filings of assets... He has made that clear in a witness statement to the High Court."

Stating that Turnberry said the president was not the owner, the KC said Trump was "being put in a degree of legal and reputational jeopardy by the position adopted by Turnberry" as it implies his previous assertions were false.

Turnberry's advocate David Massaro told the court that the company was not claiming that president's statements were false.

Massaro said Trump's stake at the course "ultimately rests in a trust in the US, and as they have averred, the president is the beneficiary".

He stated that it was his client's position that shares are held by trustees and that this is not a "sufficient link" to the company.

Sheriff Millar ordered a further hearing to take place in November and that the president be informed of the updated amount claimed by Orbis.

Steele is a director of Orbis and a former head of MI6's Russia desk.

In 2016, he was hired by a law firm linked to the Hillary Clinton presidential campaign to gather information on then-Republican nominee Trump's alleged links to Russia.

The so-called Steele dossier included a series of uncorroborated intelligence claims , including that the US president had been cultivated by Russia, that he had taken part in sex parties and had been "compromised" by the Russian security services.

The dossier was later published without permission by the website Buzzfeed in 2017.

Trump denies all the claims and launched legal action against Orbis through English courts.

In February 2024 the case brought by Trump against Orbis was thrown out.

Last April, a court ordered the president to pay Orbis more than £600,000 in legal costs.

Ayr Sheriff Court documents reveal that, due to interest, the amount sought by two applications brought by Orbis now totals £789,812.91.

The Trump family acquired the Turnberry resort in Ayrshire in June 2014.

Donald Trump was a director at the company SLC Turnberry Ltd until he resigned the position in January 2017 - a day before he was inaugurated as US president.

His sons, Don Jr and Eric, remain directors at the company.

Information held by Companies House states that Donald Trump Snr has significant control of a company called Golf Recreation Scotland, which in turn has significant control at SLC Turnberry.

A person with significant control is usually someone who has more than 25% shares or voting rights in a company, can appoint or remove a majority of directors, or can influence or control the company.

In September last year, the Daily Mail reported that sheriff officers had served legal papers at the Trump Turnberry resort.

At the time, a spokesperson for Orbis told the newspaper it was "concerned that Donald Trump continues to be in breach of the English High Court and are alarmed by the outrageous costs of this vexatious case in wasted time and money".

In court documents, Donald Trump is named as a "debtor" while it lists SLC Turnberry Limited - the company that runs the resort - is named as an "arrestee".

articles.title: Rory McIlroy falters as Aaron Rai takes joint first-round lead at Wentworth
articles.summary: Aaron Rai shoots a six-under 66 to share the first-round lead with Sweden's Joakim Lagergren at the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth as Rory McIlroy suffers a late stumble.
articles.body:
6 A Rai (Eng), J Lagergren (Swe); -5 R Gerard (US), A Scott (Aus), I Elvira (Spa), L Aberg (Swe)

Selected others : -4 P Reed (US), R Fox (NZ), R MacIntrye (Sco), V Hovland (Nor), T Detry (Bel); -3 R Fisher (Eng), R McIlroy (NI), D Law (Sco), A Sullivan (Eng), E Ferguson (Sco), J Dean (Eng); -2 T Hatton (Eng), JJ Spaun (US); -1 S Lowry (Ire) -1 M Wallace (Eng); E A Fitzpatrick (Eng), M Fitzpatrick (Eng)

While Rory McIlroy sparkled and then suffered a late stumble, Aaron Rai was a model of consistency as he shot a six-under 66 to share the first-round lead with Sweden's Joakim Lagergren at the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.

Rai, who became England's most recent major winner earlier this season , knocked in seven birdies, with the only blemish to his card arriving on the 16th, when he found the fairway bunker off the tee and ended with a bogey five.

Lagergren, whose one and only win on the DP World Tour was back in 2018, also made a fine start with an eagle on the 12th, the highlight of his round.

Six-time major winner McIlroy had got under way in sensational fashion earlier in the day until his round unravelled on the back nine.

The Northern Irishman was five under after 10 holes and in the outright lead but some erratic driving proved costly after the turn on a course he covered in 60 in Wednesday's pro-am.

And when McIlroy also found the water on his penultimate hole, it contributed to one of his three bogeys in the final seven - leaving him at three under, three strokes adrift of the joint-leaders.

American Ryan Gerard, Australia's Adam Scott, Spain's Nacho Elvira and Sweden's Ludvig Aberg are at five under, while Patrick Reed, the only player above McIlroy in the Race to Dubai standings, is one of 12 players at four under.

Reed, who is bidding to become only the second American after Collin Morikawa to win the Race to Dubai, is in a group two shots off the lead with Open champion Ryan Fox, Norway's Viktor Hovland and Scotland's Robert MacIntyre, who made birdies on the 17th and 18th holes to conclude with a flourish.

However, it was a difficult day for Spain's two-time major winner Jon Rahm, who carded a six-over 78.

Birdies proved difficult to come by as Rahm played alongside Justin Rose and Tommy Fleetwood, with none of the trio picking up a single shot on the front nine.

While the English duo were able to make five birdies between them on the back nine to finish at one over, Rahm toiled to five bogeys and a double bogey as he repeatedly found trouble off the tee.

Former US Open champion Matt Fitzpatrick, who outlined his reluctance to travel to Dubai for November's season-ending DP World Tour Championship event on Wednesday, is at level par, along with his younger brother Alex.

articles.summary: El 'León de Barrika' ocupa la penúltima plaza en el BMW PGA Championship
articles.body: Wentworth Club es uno de los escenarios más importantes del Europena Tour y el BMW PGA Championship un torneo con mucha historia en el que cinco españoles ya han inscrito su nombre en el palmarés: Manuel Piñero (1977), Severiano Ballesteros (1983 y 1991), José María Olazábal (1994), Nacho Garrido (2003) y Miguel Ángel Jiménez (2008). Jon Rahm, que ha sido dos veces segundo en este prestigioso evento del DP World Tour, firmó una vuelta para olvidar en la primera jornada. El ‘León de Barrika’ se fue a 78 golpes (+6) y ocupa la penúltima posición junto a un grupo de otros seis jugadores. Falló mucho desde el tee y los segundos golpes no ayudaron. Desde el bunker, al contrario de lo que acostumbra, no estuvo nada fino. El vizcaíno, muy impreciso hoy, ha perdido algo de fuelle desde el US Open y requerirá de una vuelta muy baja para pasar el corte, aunque quizás no tanto como aquel 62 que firmó en este campo en 2022 para casi obrar el milagro de la remontada. Sólo pudo hacer un birdie, en el hoyo 12, el único de los cuatro pares 5 del que pudo sacar tajada. El torneo lo lideran Aaron Rai –campeón este año del PGA Championship- y Joakim Lagergren con 66 golpes. La nómina de participantes en Wentworth es impresionante, de ahí que aparezcan en la tercera posición, con 67 impactos, Nacho Elvira, Ryan Gerard, Ludvig Aberg y Adam Scott. El español, que acabó con dos birdies, es décimo en el ranking que entrega 10 tarjetas para el PGA Tour, por lo que cada resultado es vital para sus aspiraciones. Por su parte, el australiano Scott podría haber terminado colíder, pero falló un putt corto para eagle en su último hoyo. El jugador en activo que más Majors seguidos ha jugado de forma consecutiva atraviesa un momento extraordinario a sus 46 años. Por detrás, con vuelta de 68, se encuentran Viktor Hovland, Ryan Fox o Patrick Reed. Por otro lado, el putter ayudó a Rory McIlroy a lograr birdies en los cuatro pares 5, aunque el driver no fue su punto fuerte en una primera ronda en la que firmó 69 golpes. Reed es el líder de la Race to Dubai con una ventaja de 841 puntos de distancia respecto al norirlandés y se podría convertir en el segundo estadounidense –tras Morikawa- que se proclama campeón anual del circuito. Entre los españoles, Manuel Elvira también está muy bien situado con 69 golpes, al igual que Alejandro del Rey. Ángel Ayora y Eugenio López-Chacarra también se sitúan en la zona alta con 70. Una pena el doble bogey del madrileño en el 18, cuando venía lanzado.

articles.title: Keisean Nixon Takes Brutally Honest Shot at Packers’ Training Camp Doubts
articles.summary: Keisean Nixon continues to be an important piece of the Green Bay Packers’ defense and special teams, serving as a primary nickel cornerback while also handl...
articles.body:
Keisean Nixon continues to be an important piece of the Green Bay Packers ' defense and special teams, serving as a primary nickel cornerback while also handling kick-return duties. In Green Bay's 39–22 season-opening loss to the Minnesota Vikings at U.S. Bank Stadium, Nixon made his presence felt with an active statistical performance on defense.

Keisean Nixon has no time for camp talk after Week 1 statement

Following the disappointing loss to Minnesota, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur highlighted Nixon's effort, describing it as one of the most complete performances he has seen from the veteran cornerback during their five seasons together.

"I just love how he competed down in and down out," LaFleur said. "There were some tough, competitive catches made on him, but he was there in coverage in a good position. Sometimes that's just how life is in the NFL, but I thought he had one of his most complete games, I would say, in my time here."

In a recent interview, Nixon was asked whether becoming the Week 1 starter ultimately validated his belief that he would remain in the starting lineup despite all the discussion surrounding the cornerback competition during training camp .

Nixon made it clear that his place on the field when the regular season began mattered far more to him than the conversations surrounding camp.

"When week one came around, where was I? Starting," Nixon said . "That's all that matters. Camp is camp. They gotta see other people get reps and stuff like that. However they felt about me during camp is irrelevant. I told you I'd be out there week one, and that's what it was.

"A lot of things don't affect me. I still came through the same process, still getting in the building at 6:30 in the morning, stacking days. Again, I can't control how they feel or how they felt during training camp."

Nixon finished the loss in Minnesota with five tackles, including three solo tackles, along with half a sack and an interception. The interception was notable because Nixon has never recorded more than one pick in a single season.

Nixon has developed significantly since beginning his Packers tenure as a reserve who primarily handled nickel responsibilities before establishing himself as an All-Pro return specialist and eventually transitioning into an outside cornerback. After previously spending time in the slot and contributing as a kick returner, Nixon became a full-time starter on the outside last season.

In 2025, Nixon started all 17 games for Green Bay while playing 1,017 defensive snaps at outside cornerback.

articles.title: Max Greyserman and Eric Cole share Round 1 lead at Biltmore Championship
articles.summary: Max Greyserman and Eric Cole are tied for the lead at 7 under in the new PGA Tour event held in Asheville.
articles.body:
ASHEVILLE, N.C. — Max Greyserman found himself in a peculiar spot, away from golf for five weeks and suddenly fighting to keep his full PGA Tour card. He responded Thursday with a 7-under 64 to share the lead with Eric Cole in the inaugural Biltmore Championship Asheville.

Greyserman got up-and-down for par on his sixth hole at The Cliff at Walnut Grove by stuffing a wedge to 2 feet, and he followed by running off four straight birdies on a rain-softened course that allowed for good scoring.

Cole, making his 131st career start on the PGA Tour and still searching for his first win, had the lead after a birdie on the par-5 eighth. But he closed out his round by finding trouble off the tee and having to punch out, ultimately missing a 20-foot par putt.

The field included seven players who will be competing in the Presidents Cup next week — five of them on the International side. Jacob Bridgeman, who makes his debut at Medinah for the U.S. team, had a 66. Nick Taylor of Canada had the leading score among Internationals at 67

The Biltmore Championship Asheville is the tour's first stop amid the Blue Ridge Mountains since Ben Hogan won in 1942. It's also the first of eight tournaments in the FedEx Cup Fall that determine the top 100 who retain full status for 2027.

That hasn't been a problem for Greyserman the last two years. The 31-year-old from New Jersey has been eligible for the last eight majors, and he has played in 12 of the $20 million signature events dating to 2025.

But he has one top 10 this year — a tie for ninth, 11 shots behind at The CJ Cup Byron Nelson — and is starts the fall series at No. 103 in the FedEx Cup. He has dropped from No. 32 in the world to start the year to No. 90.

This is his first tournament since the Wyndham Championship five weeks ago. He took off two weeks to spend time with his 8-month-old son. He headed to New Jersey for a week of a little practice, and then was gone two more weeks on a vacation to Italy.

"Maybe that's key," Greyserman said. "Don't practice and just have a good time and just show up here."

Jackson Koivun is off the tee early with Jacob Bridgeman and Webb Simpson on Friday in North Carolina. Here's how to watch Round 2 of the Biltmore Championship.

There's also the matter of a new course no one had really seen. With heavy rain and high temperatures around the Blue Ridge Mountains that caused agronomy issues, tour officials decided there would be lift, clean and place for all four rounds.

"I guess it's maybe more freeing when you play a course for the first time because you don't have any bad memories to pull up," Greyserman said. "You just have no memories, so it's nice and fresh. I think that's good."

Cole finished at No. 49 in the FedEx Cup, so he's locked into all the signature events for next year. He also loves to play golf — he has averaged 34 tournament the last three seasons — and can't think of a better place to be.

There's also the matter of trying to win. Because of a transition season in 2027 for the big PGA Tour overhaul, any winner from the eight FedEx Cup Fall events are assured of being in the Championship Series level when the new schedule begins in 2028.

"I just like to play a lot of golf. I enjoy competing," Cole said. "I worked a lot, really hard and a lot of years to get to the PGA Tour, so any chance I have to play and compete out here is something that means a lot to me, something I don't take for granted."

articles.title: Pebble Beach course change draws scorn. But critics didn't have full story
articles.summary: Justin Thomas was among critics of Pebble Beach's decision to remove a tree on the 16th hole.
articles.body:
Justin Thomas is not the Lorax but he speaks for the trees.

He thinks golf courses cut down too many of them.

Thomas said as much this week in a social-media post , citing a hole on a famous course to underscore his point: the par-4 16th at Pebble Beach Golf Links .

At 400 yards from the tips, the hole plays gently downhill from the tee, followed by an approach over a gully and between goal posts of Monterey cypress trees. At least, it used to. In early September, Pebble Beach removed the tree on the right, which stood some 90 yards short of the green.

In his commentary, Thomas criticized the change while making a broader case against tree removal.

"Such a great hole," he wrote. "Makes no sense to me why they'd do this. When are places going to realize getting rid of trees is not the answer to making courses better."

A prominent player knocking a prominent course was always going to draw attention, especially on a subject that arouses strong opinions. Tree removal has become a familiar flashpoint in an era defined by Golden Age restorations aimed at stripping courses back to the way they used to play, tree-lined corridors included.

Sure enough, armchair architects were quick to chime in. Some backed Thomas; others bashed Pebble. Still others blamed the USGA, claiming — without evidence — that the governing body ordered the tree gone to prep the course for next year's U.S. Open, which returns to Pebble Beach for the seventh time. Turns out some critics were barking up the wrong tree.

Thomas himself had committed an error of omission by failing to address the why. Courses remove trees for all kinds of reasons that have nothing to do with design philosophy. Some are agronomic: trees compete with turf for sunlight and water, they can choke off the airflow healthy grass needs, and their roots have a knack for cracking drainage pipes and cart paths. Courses plant trees for plenty of reasons, too — sometimes for strategy, but also for aesthetics, or safety, to keep golfers on tightly routed holes from getting in each other's crossfire.

In the case of the tree on the 16th at Pebble, the USGA had nothing to do with it. A spokesperson for the government made that plain in an email to GOLF , and Pebble Beach corroborated it.

The real explanation for removing the tree, a Pebble Beach spokesperson wrote in an email, was health. The tree "had become diseased and infested beyond recovery, despite our best efforts to treat it over the past two years. It was removed upon recommendation from a local certified arborist to prevent the risk of spreading to neighboring trees."

Courses lose trees all the time, and Pebble is no exception. This past spring, the resort replaced a Cypress tree in the 18th fairway that had been toppled in a 2014 storm. In 2002, an 80-foot Monterey cypress was planted beside the 18th green, taken from the 1st hole to replace the original, which had died of pitch canker disease.

That transplanting — digging a giant hole, maneuvering a giant root ball into a place — was something of a spectacle. But it wasn't spread and distorted by social media.

The facts are these: The tree is gone, and it was removed because it was sick. Reasonable people can disagree as to whether the hole is better or worse without it. Pebble Beach told GOLF that it will stay in touch with its arborist about the possibility of planting something new in its place. That's TBD. If it remains a bare spot, count on Justin Thomas being asked about it at the U.S. Open next year.
